extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, compliance officers, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the regulatory standards and definitional criteria the Department of Education uses under Title IX for sex-based harassment, specific offenses (sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, stalking), consent, jurisdiction, and recipient obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile environment sex-based harassment definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostile environment sex-based harassment is defined as unwelcome sex-based conduct that, based on the totality of the circumstances, is subjectively and objectively offensive and is so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies a person's ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient's education program or activity (i.e., creates a hostile environment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a hostile environment has been created is a fact-specific inquiry. The Department cites Davis (526 U.S. at 651) endorsing a 'totality of the circumstances' assessment. The definition contemplates and requires application of administrator judgment; it is not incompatible with elementary or secondary contexts because it accounts for parties' ages and objective offensiveness. The Department also notes that unwelcome sex-based conduct that is severe or pervasive and meets the other elements would constitute sex-based harassment under Title IX, and a single instance of sexual assault would likely meet the hostile-environment definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in assessing hostile environment (totality of circumstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment must consider, among other things, the degree to which the conduct affected the complainant's ability to access the education program or activity; the type, frequency, and duration of the conduct; the parties' ages, roles within the recipient's education program or activity, previous interactions, and other relevant factors about each party; the location of the conduct and the context in which it occurred; and other sex-based harassment in the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes this is a fact-specific inquiry; these enumerated factors narrow scope and allow consideration appropriate to elementary/secondary settings. The Department draws on Davis's 'constellation of surrounding circumstances, expectations, and relationships' standard. Recipients should weigh these elements in context rather than apply a rigid checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated events rule (single-incident severity requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that is an isolated event must be so severe that it limits or denies participation in an activity to constitute hostile environment sex-based harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble clarifies that a single instance may qualify if sufficiently severe (the Davis Court acknowledged single instances can have systemic effects). However, the regulations also distinguish administrative enforcement from private litigation standards for monetary damages. Recipients should not assume that all single incidents automatically create a hostile environment; severity and effect on access are key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific offenses included as sex-based harassment (textual inclusion vs cross-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of 'sex-based harassment' includes textual definitions of specific offenses (sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking) largely aligned with the Clery Act, included in the Title IX regulations' text rather than by cross-reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department opted to include textual definitions for readability and to avoid requiring recipients to consult other statutes. It acknowledges potential future statutory changes may require technical updates. Inclusion is intended to be consistent with the Clery Act, though small Title IX-specific adjustments (e.g., to domestic violence language) were made where VAWA language is not applicable to Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific offenses need not satisfy hostile-environment elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the final regulations, the specific offenses of sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking need not satisfy the elements of severity or pervasiveness or subjective and objective offensiveness in order to constitute sex-based harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department confirms these specific offenses are based on federally validated definitions and thus are treated as sex-based harassment without requiring the hostile-environment element test. The specific offenses also need not satisfy the element of unwelcomeness. Whether certain misdemeanor sexual assaults were dismissed in civil suits is not dispositive for these administrative regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual assault definition (Clery Act/FBI UCR tracking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of sexual assault mirrors the Clery Act's statutory definition (20 U.S.C. 1092(f)(6)(A)(v)) by reference to the FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) system/NIBRS definitions, which include rape, sodomy, sexual assault with an object, fondling, incest, and statutory rape—conduct 'without the consent of the victim, including instances where the victim is incapable of giving consent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to restate the FBI definitions in full but retains the statutory reference to the UCR to maintain consistency with the Clery Act and VAWA 2022. The use of terms 'forcible' and 'nonforcible' in the text is retained for statutory consistency and is not intended to imply that force is required; lack of consent is the relevant consideration. Recipients may provide examples and training and consider complainant age when classifying incidents. Unwelcome sex-based conduct meeting hostile-environment elements also constitutes sex-based harassment regardless of whether it meets a specific offense definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent: Departmental non-definition / recipient discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to adopt a Federal definition of 'consent' for Title IX purposes and will not require a recipient to adopt a particular definition of consent; recipients may define 'consent' in their policies consistent with applicable State law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will include a note that the Assistant Secretary will not require a recipient to adopt a particular definition. Recipients may consider age, developmental level, and disability laws in any definition. The Department rejects the notion that omitting a federal definition shifts burdens; §106.45(f)(1) requires the recipient—and not the parties—to gather sufficient evidence to determine whether sex discrimination occurred, so recipients may not shift the burden of proof to respondents or complainants. Training required under the final regulations must include any definitions used by the recipient (including consent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of student disability records and consultation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a complainant or respondent is an elementary or secondary student with a disability, the Title IX Coordinator must consult with one or more members of the student's IEP team and one or more members of the Section 504 team, if any, to help ensure compliance with IDEA and Section 504 throughout grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some evidence relevant to capacity to consent may be records maintained by treating professionals; final regulations at §106.45(b)(7)(ii) prohibit use of such records in grievance procedures unless the eligible student or parent provides voluntary, written consent. Recipients must obtain that consent before using those records to aid determinations regarding consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional scope of Title IX enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX applies to sex discrimination, including sex-based harassment, occurring under a recipient's education program or activity in the United States. Sex-based harassment that occurs outside of a recipient's education program or activity does not trigger Title IX, except where it contributes to a hostile environment that exists under the recipient's program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department disagrees that specific offenses are covered regardless of where they occur. However, §106.11 requires a recipient to address a hostile environment that exists under its education program or activity even when some contributing conduct occurred outside the recipient's program or activity. Recipients should evaluate whether out-of-program conduct contributes to an in-program hostile environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dating violence definition alignment with VAWA 2022
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department revised the proposed definition of dating violence in the final regulations to align fully with VAWA 2022's definition (34 U.S.C. 12291(a)(11)), which defines dating violence as violence committed by a person who is or has been in a social relationship of a romantic or intimate nature with the victim, with existence of such a relationship determined by length, type, and frequency of interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final definition does not require dating violence to be a 'crime of violence.' The Department declined suggestions to merge dating and domestic violence definitions or to import additional VAWA victim-services language that is inapplicable to Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic violence definition adjustments and interaction with VAWA/HUD
rubrics_metrics.description: The Title IX domestic violence definition does not incorporate all language from VAWA 2022; the Department removed language concerning 'victim services' (inapplicable to Title IX) and removed the phrase 'of violence' to better align with VAWA 2022's intent. The definition still refers to felony and misdemeanor crimes in the recipient's jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains omission of certain VAWA language is to avoid confusion and is not intended to preclude finding sex-based harassment based on coercive or controlling behavior. Conduct such as repeated coercive behavior may constitute sex-based harassment if based on sex and meeting hostile-environment elements. Recipients subject to other federal agency rules (e.g., HUD) must comply with Title IX regulations as well as any applicable other-agency regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific-offense format and interplay with consent/intent concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific offenses (sexual assault, etc.) are based on other federally validated definitions and are not written in the same format as quid pro quo or hostile environment definitions; reference to sexual assault introduces concepts of consent (as in the FBI/UCR definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department acknowledges the difference in format and that inclusion of sexual assault brings consent considerations into the Title IX analysis via the underlying federal offense definitions, but reiterates that recipients retain discretion regarding consent definitions for policy purposes. The presence of consent concepts in specific-offense definitions does not permit recipients to shift evidentiary burdens away from themselves.
